_README: WAVE ROSTERS and SERIALIZATION GROUPS for the bookworm -> trixie migration.
registry/bridge-suites.json says WHICH suite each tile is on. This file says
in what ORDER tiles are migrated and, more importantly, WHICH TILES MUST NOT
BUILD AT THE SAME TIME. Until now both lived only as prose -- the wave table
in docs/lab/BRIDGE-TRIXIE-MIGRATION.md section 4 and a blockquote in the
session handover -- so every wave agent re-read them, and nothing enforced
them. scripts/dev/migrate-wave.sh reads this file instead.
The wave table in BRIDGE-TRIXIE-MIGRATION.md section 4 is still the plan of
record and the place to argue about ordering; `waves` below is its machine-
readable form. migrate-wave.sh prints the roster it read, so a divergence is
visible rather than silent, and it REFUSES to run when a tile here is absent
from the ledger or when a ledger tile appears in no wave at all.
`serialization` is the load-bearing half. A group's tiles hold ONE claim, so
at most one of them builds at a time -- across concurrent agents, not just
within one wave, because the claim is taken on the box. `tiles` is not a
hand list to be trusted: migrate-wave.sh DERIVES the membership from the
builders (see `derivation`) and refuses to run if the two disagree, so a new
chroot tile cannot join the fleet without joining the group.
Not generated: never run stations-registry.py against it. Same rule as
registry/bridge-suites.json, and for the same reason.

unwaved.indyr4400: Not in the section 4 wave table, and that gap is real rather than an oversight to paper over here: it is the box's largest CPU consumer (319% of a core), it is deliberately STOPPED by the operator, and the plan doc's advice for tiles of its shape is to run it alone. Give it its own wave when the operator restores it.

mame-chroot.resource: the suite's mameChroot -- registry/bridge-suites.json suites.<suite>.mameChroot, i.e. /data/vms/sandbox/trixie-chroot for trixie
mame-chroot.why: All the MAME builders chroot into the SAME directory and mount API filesystems inside it. Two concurrent builds doing that is the failure class that took the host's /dev/pts down and broke every new interactive login on the box for hours (AGENTS.md, the PTY-allocation-failed row). chroot-guard fixed the mount-propagation half; this claim is the who-owns-it half. ccache -- not parallelism -- is what makes a MAME wave cheap: 59.1% on the first cold build and 96-100% on every tree after it, so serializing these costs almost nothing.
mame-chroot.derivation: a tile is a member iff scripts/build-guests/tiles/<tile>.sh names an emulators/build-mame-*.sh helper that itself calls bridge_mame_chroot_for
